benchmark_name: Synthetic Speech, Real Signal: Paralinguistic Preservation and Cross-Lingual Augmentation via Voice Cloning
authors: Roseline Polle; Owen Parsons; George Fairs; Luis M San Martin Fernandez; Cole Looney; Xiaoliang Wu; Alexandra L Georgescu; Stefano Goria
institutions: thymia, UK; The University of Edinburgh, UK; University of Southampton, UK
ground_truth_source: PHQ-8 score ≥10 + self-reported prior diagnosis (depression); GAD-7 score ≥10 + self-reported prior diagnosis (anxiety); dataset labels for public tasks (IEMOCAP, MELD, MUSTARD, VCTK)
size_of_benchmark: Public: IEMOCAP 5,531; MELD 13,708; MUSTARD 690; VCTK 29,650; Proprietary EN 82,046 samples (30,537 speakers); Proprietary JP 14,159 samples (6,253 speakers)
what_assessed_skills: Paralinguistic signal preservation through voice cloning; depression and anxiety detection from speech; emotion recognition; sentiment classification; sarcasm detection; accent classification; cross-lingual transfer of clinical speech biomarkers
tasks_assessed: Depression detection (binary); Anxiety detection (binary); Emotion recognition (4-class, IEMOCAP); Emotion recognition (7-class, MELD); Sentiment classification (3-class, MELD); Sarcasm detection (binary, MUSTARD); Accent classification (3-class, VCTK)
population_represented: English clinical: 30,537 speakers (F/M=60/40%, mean age=37, White/Black/Asian/Mixed=70/15/7/5%); Japanese clinical: 6,253 speakers (F/M/unspecified=40/50/10%, mean age=51, Asian/Other/unspecified=85/5/10%)
evaluation_method: Automated. WavLM Large embeddings (1024-dim) + Logistic Regression classifier; 5-fold stratified group cross-validation; AUC (one-vs-rest, macro-averaged for multi-class); preservation score P=(Ac−0.5)/(Ar−0.5); permutation test vs. chance; paired bootstrap test (cloned vs. real); paired z-test for cross-lingual conditions; Pearson correlation between speaker similarity and AUC degradation.
llms_evaluated: None (paper evaluates voice cloning models, not LLMs; Qwen3 235B used only for translation preprocessing)
performance_scores: RQ1 (monolingual): Real AUC on public tasks mean=0.785; best cloning model (repeat) mean=0.768 (E2-TTS); median degradation 3.2 pp; median preservation P=0.87; clinical corpus top models P=0.93–0.94. RQ2 (cross-lingual, N=10,000): Raw EN→JP: depression AUC=0.593, anxiety=0.578; best cloned: OpenAudio depression=0.626, CosyVoice3 anxiety=0.618; in-language JP: depression=0.654, anxiety=0.664. RQ3: Speaker similarity vs. AUC degradation Pearson r=0.87 (clinical general), r=0.81 (mood), r=0.77 (paragraph), r=0.87 (IEMOCAP).
short_summary: This paper investigates whether voice cloning models preserve paralinguistic signal relevant to clinical tasks such as depression and anxiety detection, and whether cloned speech can augment cross-lingual training data. Eight open-source voice cloning models (XTTS v2, Zonos, E2-TTS, F5-TTS, OpenAudio S1-mini, CosyVoice 2, CosyVoice 3, MaskGCT) are benchmarked on five paralinguistic tasks across four public datasets and one proprietary clinical English/Japanese corpus. WavLM Large embeddings and logistic regression are used with AUC as the primary metric, evaluated via stratified cross-validation and bootstrap tests. Results show that most cloning models preserve the majority of paralinguistic signal (median degradation 3.2 pp; best models P≥0.90), and that training on English speech cloned into Japanese significantly outperforms raw cross-lingual transfer for depression and anxiety detection, suggesting voice cloning is a viable augmentation strategy for low-resource clinical speech settings.

benchmark_name: What Clinicians Need: Designing, Developing and Evaluating an AI-Based Decision Support System for Autism Assessment
authors: Ulrike Schäfer; William Saakyan; Matthias Norden; Fabrizio Kuruc; Peter Sörries; Isabel Dziobek; Claudia Müller-Birn; Hanna Drimalla
institutions: Freie Universität Berlin, Germany; Bielefeld University, Germany; Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, Germany
ground_truth_source: Two real patient cases (one ASC, one Non-ASC) chosen by experienced clinicians based on diagnostic assessments; patients provided informed consent. AI model trained on 325 adult participants (168 ASC, 157 Non-ASC) with IRB-approved clinical diagnoses.
size_of_benchmark: 7 clinicians (formative study); 7 clinicians (evaluation study); 2 patient cases assessed at 3 decision points = 42 decisions total
what_assessed_skills: Clinician decision-making accuracy and reasoning when assisted by AI-based CDSS; ability to interpret nonverbal behavior visualizations (gaze, facial expressions, voice); formation of mental models of AI; appropriateness of AI reliance (over-reliance, under-reliance)
tasks_assessed: ASC vs. Non-ASC binary screening decision at three decision points (after SIT video, after data-based assessment, after model-based AI recommendation); think-aloud reasoning about nonverbal behavior; prediction of AI recommendation
population_represented: Adult patients (ASC and Non-ASC); clinicians/psychotherapists of varying experience levels (formative and evaluation studies)
languages: German (interviews conducted in German, based on institutional context; not explicitly stated)
evaluation_method: Human evaluation — 7 clinicians assessed 2 patient cases at 3 sequential decision points each (42 total decisions); think-aloud protocols and semi-structured interviews; inductive/deductive qualitative coding of ~8 hours of transcripts; decision path categorization (consistent AI-confirmed, consistent not AI-confirmed, uncertain-to-aligned, ambiguous). Metrics: decision path type, decision changes across DPs, qualitative mental model themes, clinician feedback ratings.
mental_health_conditions: Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC) / Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)
performance_scores: AI model (XGBoost late-fusion): accuracy 74%, precision 0.76, recall 0.74 (Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation on 325 participants). Clinician study: 7 of 14 decision paths showed consistent AI-confirmed decisions; 3 paths showed consistent non-AI-confirmed decisions; 2 paths changed from uncertain to aligning with AI; 2 paths showed decisions under ambiguity.
short_summary: This paper designs, develops, and evaluates SIT-CARE, a human-centered AI-based clinical decision support system (CDSS) for autism spectrum condition (ASC) screening in adults. The system uses nonverbal behavioral data (gaze, facial expressions, voice) extracted from standardized video interactions (Simulated Interaction Task) and provides clinicians with data visualizations and an XGBoost-based AI recommendation. A formative study with 7 clinicians identified 5 key challenges and design strategies; an evaluation study with 7 newly recruited clinicians assessed how SIT-CARE influenced decision-making across 3 sequential decision points per patient case. Four distinct decision path types were identified, revealing varied mental models and reliance patterns. The study does not evaluate LLMs; the AI component is a classical ML model (XGBoost).

benchmark_name: Analysing Self-Harm Representations in Language Models: a Cross-Architecture Study
ground_truth_source: Two datasets: (1) X-Sensitive (Antypas et al., 2025) — multi-label social media posts annotated for sensitive content categories including self-harm; (2) SH-Detection (Tharsi, 2025) — HuggingFace dataset with class="self-harm" labels. Both used as-is with binary self-harm vs. control splits.
size_of_benchmark: 400 posts (X-Sensitive: 200 self-harm + 200 control); 600 posts (SH-Detection: balanced binary)
what_assessed_skills: Internal representation of self-harm content across LLM layers; linear separability of self-harm vs. control posts in residual stream activations; geometric stability of contrastive self-harm directions across network depth
tasks_assessed: Layer-wise linear probing for self-harm detection; contrastive direction extraction and analysis; cross-layer directional stability measurement
population_represented: Social media users posting self-harm related content (English-language posts)
evaluation_method: Automated. Linear probes (L2-regularised logistic regression) trained on residual stream activations at each layer, evaluated via 5-fold stratified cross-validation. Primary metric: mean ROC-AUC. Contrastive direction separability measured via Cohen's d. Directional stability assessed via pairwise cosine similarity matrices across layers.
performance_scores: X-Sensitive best probe ROC-AUC: Qwen3-0.6B=0.703±0.016, Llama 3.2-1B=0.808±0.040, Llama 3.2-3B=0.804±0.040, Gemma-3-4B=0.817±0.050. SH-Detection best probe ROC-AUC: Qwen3-0.6B=0.923±0.017, Llama 3.2-1B=0.952±0.011, Llama 3.2-3B=0.972±0.011, Gemma-3-4B=0.969±0.012. Self-harm concepts crystallize at 93–97% network depth across all models.
short_summary: This paper analyzes how four open-source LLMs internally represent self-harm content using representation engineering techniques on two social media datasets. The study trains linear probes across all layers of each model and extracts contrastive self-harm directions to understand where and how self-harm concepts are encoded. Models tested include Qwen3-0.6B, Llama 3.2-1B-Instruct, Llama 3.2-3B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-4B-it, evaluated on the X-Sensitive and SH-Detection datasets using ROC-AUC and Cohen's d metrics (fully automated). Key findings are that self-harm information consistently crystallizes in the final 3–7% of network layers, contrastive directions are not stable across depth (block-diagonal structure), and Gemma-3-4B exhibits high classification accuracy despite lower geometric separability, suggesting its self-harm signal is distributed across the activation space rather than concentrated in one direction.
